newsitem.title: USA: Boeing confident of McDonnell merger by August.
newsitem.headline: Boeing confident of McDonnell merger by August.

text.p: Boeing Co. Chairman Phil Condit said Tuesday he was confident the company's merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp. would be completed in July or August.
Condit told reporters before a Town Hall meeting here he does not expect a European Commission probe to derail the merger.
He said European regulators and the U.S. Federal Trade Commission were asking "classic competitive questions, the kind of things you'd expect them to be asking."
On Monday European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told Reuters he may have under-rated the problems with the planned merger and that he would launch a full investigation into the deal.
Seattle-based Boeing and St. Louis-based McDonnell Douglas agreed to merge in December in a deal valued at about $15 billion.
Condit said concerns from some quarters that Boeing and European consortium Airbus Industrie might somehow get together to "gouge the customer" were unfounded.
He said a number of coutries have expressed an interest in competing with the two companies for market share including China, South Korea, Japan, Russia and Indonesia.
Condit said no decision had been reached on whether or not Boeing would continue producing McDonnell Douglas commercial aircraft should the merger get regulatory approval.
"The market will make that determination," he said. "If we can make the McDonnell Douglas line at good margins then we will keep on doing it."
He said Boeing has a net profit margin of 4.5 percent to 5 percent on its commercial aircraft production and that he would like to see that margin rise to 6 percent to 8 percent.
Condit said the case to continue production of McDonnell's MD-95 aircraft seemed strong.
"I believe that if cost levels can be achieved there ought to be a very good market (for the MD-95)," he said.

The MD-95 is McDonnell's latest aircraft which seats about 100 passengers. To date troubled discount airline ValuJet Inc. is the aircraft's biggest customer ordering 50 MD-95's and taking an option to buy a further 50.
"Over the past couple of years McDonnell Douglas has not been particularly effective (in getting orders)," he said.

Condit said no concrete decisions had been made on what models to keep because McDonnell Douglas and Boeing were precluded from sharing competition-sensitive information before the merger gets regulatory approval.
The merger would probably result in minimal lay-offs of McDonnell Douglas staff, he said, adding that efficiencies could be largely met through natural work force attrition.
Condit said that Boeing, which hired 21,000 employees last year, would probably only see a modest rise in staff this year.
